screens.title: Advanced Testing Patterns & Strategies
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we build a practical toolkit for testing harder smart contract scenarios. You will learn how to manipulate blockchain time, take and restore EVM snapshots for fast isolated tests, measure gas in assertions, and mock external dependencies so tests stay focused and reliable. These techniques matter because real contracts often depend on time windows, on-chain state machines, or external services; naive tests miss subtle failures or become slow and flaky. For example, a time-locked vault must be tested both before and after an unlock timestamp; using the Hardhat RPC methods for advancing time and mining a block lets you simulate that passage reliably. Snapshotting saves a configured global state once and reverts to it between tests, making large setups fast to reuse. Gas checks in tests help you catch regressions in critical functions, and lightweight mocks let you control or simulate token transfers or oracle responses without deploying full systems. As you study the examples and activity, watch for common mistakes, like forgetting to mine after increasing time or neglecting to account for gas when checking balances. By the end you'll be able to pick the right pattern for time-based logic, costly setups, gas-sensitive functions, and external interactions. Consider where each technique could make your own test suite faster, less flaky, and more trustworthy.

Module 06 › Chapter 6.4 › Advanced Testing Patterns
Advanced Testing Patterns & Strategies
Use Hardhat's EVM controls, snapshots, gas checks, and mocks to make tests accurate and fast.
In this lesson
Simulate time, snapshot the EVM, analyze gas, and mock dependencies so your smart contract tests reflect production behavior without becoming slow or brittle.
Coming up
Hands-on examples include a TimeLockVault test that fast-forwards time and an Auction activity that demonstrates a full time-based flow with assertions and event checks.
Starter takeaway

These patterns reduce flakiness and speed tests: time control for temporal logic, snapshotting for expensive setups, gas checks for regressions, and mocks for external dependencies.

Concept Map
Time control → Snapshots → Gas checks → Mocks
Time control
Snapshotting
Gas checks
Mocking
Explore Key Topics
Time-dependent logic
Fast-forward the EVM to test unlocks, vesting, and auctions without waiting in real time.
EVM snapshotting
Save and revert EVM state to reuse expensive setups and keep tests isolated and fast.
Mocking & Gas analysis
Use lightweight mocks for external contracts and assert gas thresholds to catch regressions.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: Over the next screens we focus on four practical objectives. First, implement tests for time-dependent logic: you will learn how to change the EVM timestamp and mine a block so contracts that depend on block time behave predictably in tests. Second, apply EVM snapshotting to create fast, isolated test scenarios for expensive setups; you'll save state once and revert for each test to avoid redeploying complex systems. Third, write tests that simulate gas cost analysis: capture gas used in receipts and assert thresholds so critical functions don't regress. Fourth, explore strategies for testing interactions and when to use mocking or stubbing; mocks allow you to isolate your contract from full external dependencies. Each objective includes a short mnemonic to help embed the idea: think 'Time then Mine', 'Snapshot and Revert', 'Measure Gas', and 'Mock for Focus'. These skills reduce flakiness, speed up CI runs, and make test failures easier to diagnose. By the end you'll be able to plan a test strategy for common contract patterns like vaults, auctions, and factory systems.

screens.title: Testing time-dependent logic
screens.narratorSegment: Temporal logic appears whenever a contract checks block timestamps or block numbers. A reliable test pattern has a few steps: detect the time-dependent requirement, arrange initial state, advance the EVM time, mine a block to apply the change, and then assert behavior and emitted events. Start by identifying the time boundary—unlockTime, auctionEndTime, or a vesting cliff. Arrange the contract in the desired pre-condition by calling deposit or placing bids so the state is meaningful. Then use the Hardhat RPC call to increase the EVM time by the required duration. Remember that increasing time alone does not change the chain until you mine a block; you must call the provider's mine method to create a block with the new timestamp. After mining, re-check the contract state and perform the action you want to test, such as withdraw or endAuction. Finally, assert on state changes, events, and balances. Include gas accounting if balance assertions are sensitive to gas costs. A common misconception is assuming that evm_increaseTime immediately changes block. timestamp without mining; tests that miss the mine step will silently fail to exercise the time condition. As a concrete example, take a vault with unlockTime set to now plus seven days: deposit funds, attempt withdrawal to confirm revert, evm_increaseTime by seven days plus one second, evm_mine, then withdraw and assert lockedAmount is zero, the recipient received funds, and a FundsUnlocked event fired. The key takeaway: always mine a block after changing time and include gas-aware assertions when verifying balances to avoid flaky tests.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.4 › Testing time-dependent logic
Step-by-step
  1. Identify the time boundary (unlockTime, auctionEndTime).
  2. Arrange preconditions (deposit, place bids) so the state is meaningful.
  3. Advance time with evm_increaseTime and then evm_mine to apply it.
  4. Act on the contract (withdraw, endAuction) and capture the transaction receipt.
  5. Assert state changes, events, and balances, using closeTo for gas-aware balance checks.
Common mistake
Forgetting to call evm_mine after evm_increaseTime. The timestamp won't apply until a new block is mined.
Concrete example (visual)
Scenario: TimeLockVault with a 7-day lock.
// Arrange: deposit 10 ETH
await timeLockVault.deposit({ value: ethers.utils.parseEther("10") });
// Act/Simulate: increase time then mine
await ethers.provider.send("evm_increaseTime", [initialLockDuration + 1]);
await ethers.provider.send("evm_mine");
// Act: withdraw and assert
const tx = await timeLockVault.connect(owner).withdraw();
const receipt = await tx.wait();
console.log("Gas used:", receipt.gasUsed.toString());
Key takeaway
Time manipulation requires a mined block. Always include balance assertions that account for gas when checking transfers.

screens.title: TimeLockVault test walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a concrete test for the TimeLockVault contract. The test first deploys the contract with a seven-day lock and deposits funds so there is a meaningful lockedAmount. The first assertion attempts a withdrawal immediately and expects a revert with the message 'Funds are still locked'. This verifies the precondition. The second test simulates waiting by calling the provider's evm_increaseTime with the lock duration plus one second, then calls evm_mine to ensure the next block reflects the new timestamp. After mining, the test calls withdraw and awaits the transaction receipt. From the receipt it obtains gasUsed and multiplies by the effectiveGasPrice to measure the cost deducted from the owner's balance. The test then asserts that lockedAmount is zero, that the owner's balance increased by the withdrawn amount minus gas used using a closeTo assertion, and that the FundsUnlocked event was emitted with expected arguments. A key point is the gas-aware balance assertion: because the owner pays gas on withdraw, exact equality will fail; using closeTo with a small delta prevents flaky failures. A common misconception is to compare raw balances without subtracting gas or using a tolerant comparison. Another important detail is deploying contracts and calling deposit in beforeEach so each test starts with its own fresh contract state. Reflect: when would you prefer snapshotting over redeploying? That question guides the next pattern we explore.

keyIdea.title: What to check in time tests
keyIdea.text: Expect reverts before unlock, simulate time + mine, assert state zeroed, check balances accounting for gas, and verify event emission.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.4 › TimeLockVault Test
Key test structure
beforeEach: deploy contract, deposit funds. Test A: expect revert. Test B: increase time, mine, withdraw and assert.
it("Should allow withdrawal after unlock time", async function () {
  await ethers.provider.send("evm_increaseTime", [initialLockDuration + 1]);
  await ethers.provider.send("evm_mine");

  const initialOwnerBalance = await ethers.provider.getBalance(owner.address);
  const lockedAmount = await timeLockVault.lockedAmount();

  const tx = await timeLockVault.connect(owner).withdraw();
  const receipt = await tx.wait();
  const gasUsed = receipt.gasUsed.mul(receipt.effectiveGasPrice);

  expect(await timeLockVault.lockedAmount()).to.equal(0);
  expect(await ethers.provider.getBalance(owner.address))
    .to.be.closeTo(initialOwnerBalance.add(lockedAmount).sub(gasUsed), ethers.utils.parseEther("0.0001"));
  await expect(tx)
    .to.emit(timeLockVault, "FundsUnlocked")
    .withArgs(lockedAmount, owner.address);
});
Explanation & tips
  • Capture the receipt to get gasUsed and effectiveGasPrice for gas-aware assertions.
  • Use closeTo for balance comparisons when gas is involved to avoid flakiness.
  • Remember: evm_increaseTime without evm_mine won't apply the new timestamp.
Takeaway
Structure time tests to show the failing precondition, simulate time properly, and then assert results including gas impact.

screens.title: EVM Snapshotting
screens.narratorSegment: EVM snapshotting saves the current state of the Hardhat Network so you can revert to it later. The typical pattern is to perform an expensive setup once in a global before hook — for example, deploy a factory and preload data — then call evm_snapshot just before a test, store the returned snapshot id, and after the test call evm_revert with that id. Reverting returns the chain to the exact saved state, making each test start from identical conditions without redeploying everything. This approach is much faster than running the full setup in beforeEach for heavy configurations. A concrete example: deploy a complex marketplace in before, then in beforeEach call snapshot and in afterEach revert. One misconception is to rely solely on before for setup and skip snapshotting; that causes tests to run against modified shared state and introduces interdependence and flakiness. Another mistake is using snapshots incorrectly by forgetting to reassign a new snapshot id for each test, which can lead to reverting to an older state inadvertently. Snapshotting is especially valuable when combined with other patterns: use snapshots after you arrange a preconfigured scenario, then within individual tests you can safely manipulate time, mock dependencies, or assert gas without worrying about cleanup. Remember that snapshots are a testing-only convenience provided by the Hardhat Network and are not available in production environments.

keyIdea.title: Snapshot principle
keyIdea.text: Use evm_snapshot before a test and evm_revert after to reuse a costly setup and ensure each test starts from the same EVM state.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.4 › EVM Snapshotting
What is a snapshot?
A snapshot stores the entire in-memory EVM state so you can return to it quickly using evm_revert.
before(async function () {
  // expensive global setup
  // deploy factory, preload assets
});

beforeEach(async function () {
  snapshotId = await ethers.provider.send("evm_snapshot", []);
});

afterEach(async function () {
  await ethers.provider.send("evm_revert", [snapshotId]);
});
Use snapshots to speed up test suites where the initial configuration is costly to create but identical across many tests.
Guidelines & pitfalls
  • Take a new snapshot for each test run to avoid reusing old IDs incorrectly.
  • Reverting restores balances, storage, and deployed contracts to the saved state.
  • Snapshots are testing conveniences only; they don't exist in production networks.
Misconception
Snapshots are not a substitute for good test isolation design; they are a performance optimization for heavy setups.

screens.title: Snapshot usage in test suites
screens.narratorSegment: This lesson demonstrates a practical snapshot usage pattern inside a describe block. Run expensive setup once in a before hook: deploy a factory, configure roles, or mint many tokens. Then in beforeEach call the provider's evm_snapshot and store the returned id in a variable. This makes the following test start from the exact configured state. After each test, call evm_revert passing the snapshot id to return to the pre-test state. This pattern avoids redeploying heavy contracts repeatedly while still giving each test a clean slate. A concrete scenario: deploy a marketplace with multiple collections and liquidity in before, take a snapshot in beforeEach, then in tests modify balances, run auctions, or change approvals without affecting other tests because afterEach reverts the chain. One nuance: if a test itself calls evm_snapshot, track and revert that snapshot before returning to the suite-level snapshot. Another mistake is to reuse a single global snapshot id across multiple tests without reassigning it in beforeEach; this causes tests to rollback to an old state and can be confusing. Snapshotting pairs well with time manipulation and mocks: take the snapshot after mocking and configuring the scenario, then within the test you can fast-forward time or alter mocked return values and revert afterward. The closing question: which part of your current slow test setup could become a one-time before hook followed by snapshots?

keyIdea.title: Snapshot practice
keyIdea.text: Perform heavy setup once, snapshot before each test, revert after each test, and avoid reusing stale snapshot ids.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.4 › Snapshot Usage
Pattern
Use before for expensive one-time setup, beforeEach to snapshot, afterEach to revert.
before(async function () {
  // heavy setup only once
});

beforeEach(async function () {
  snapshotId = await ethers.provider.send("evm_snapshot", []);
});

afterEach(async function () {
  await ethers.provider.send("evm_revert", [snapshotId]);
});
Practical tips
  • Take snapshots after all mocks and configs are in place so each test inherits them.
  • Track snapshot ids carefully if nested snapshots are used inside tests.
  • Use snapshotting to speed up suites that would otherwise redeploy identical state repeatedly.
Pitfall
Reverting to the wrong snapshot id can hide test failures. Always reassign snapshotId in beforeEach.

screens.title: Snapshotting vs. beforeEach redeploy
screens.narratorSegment: Both snapshotting and redeploying beforeEach yield isolated tests, but they trade off speed and reproducibility differently. Redeploying in beforeEach gives each test a completely fresh set of contracts and is conceptually simple. It is ideal for small setups where deployment is cheap and you want maximum isolation. Snapshotting, by contrast, is a performance optimization: deploy or configure a large system once, take a snapshot, and revert to it between tests. This is much faster for complex environments but requires careful snapshot id management. A concrete example highlights the trade: a test suite that deploys a multi-contract factory and populates it with many tokens will grow slow if redeployed for every test. Using a before hook to build the system and snapshotting in beforeEach makes individual tests run quickly. A common misconception is that snapshotting reduces the need to design isolated tests; it does not. Snapshots restore state but do not replace good test boundaries. Another mistake is using snapshots when deployments are cheap; you risk adding complexity without a speed benefit. When deciding, ask: is the setup expensive and identical across tests? If yes, snapshot. If each test requires a different deployment configuration, redeploying in beforeEach is clearer and safer. The final takeaway: choose the simpler approach unless performance demands the optimization.

keyIdea.text: Use beforeEach redeploy for small, clear setups; use snapshotting when a costly common setup must be reused for many tests.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.4 › Snapshot vs Redeploy
Redeploy (beforeEach)
  • Simple and explicit; each test gets fresh contracts.
  • Best when deployments are cheap or tests require different configs.
  • Less chance of accidental state carryover.
Snapshot (before + snapshot)
  • Faster for suites with an expensive identical setup.
  • Requires careful snapshot id handling and understanding of revert behavior.
  • Pairs well with mocks and time manipulation done after the snapshot.
Decision checklist
Is setup expensive?
Are configs identical?
Do tests need fresh deployments?

screens.title: Gas cost analysis in tests
screens.narratorSegment: Gas analysis in tests helps you prevent regressions in critical contract functions. The common pattern is to send a transaction, wait for its receipt, read receipt. gasUsed, and compare that value against a chosen threshold. Start by identifying functions where gas matters — loops, token transfers in batches, or frequently called public functions. In your test, call the function, await tx. wait(), and then read receipt. gasUsed. If you want to analyze cost in currency terms, multiply gasUsed by receipt. effectiveGasPrice to compute the native token cost. Be cautious: gas numbers can vary slightly across environments, so assert conservative thresholds rather than exact numbers. For example, assert that gasUsed is less than one hundred thousand units for a simple withdraw function, or check that a refactor doesn't increase gas beyond an acceptable delta. Log gasUsed during local runs to build a baseline before asserting. A common misconception is to use gas assertions as the only indicator of efficiency; gas checks complement profiling tools and should flag regressions but not replace in-depth performance analysis. Also remember that gas costs can depend on storage layout and prior state; ensure tests set up consistent conditions. The practical result: automated gas checks catch accidental expensive changes early and keep critical paths optimized.

The common pattern is to send a transaction, wait for its receipt, read receipt. gasUsed, and compare that value against a chosen threshold. Start by identifying functions where gas matters — loops, token transfers in batches, or frequently called public functions. In your test, call the function, await tx. wait(), and then read receipt. gasUsed. If you want to analyze cost in currency terms, multiply gasUsed by receipt. effectiveGasPrice to compute the native token cost. Be cautious: gas numbers can vary slightly across environments, so assert conservative thresholds rather than exact numbers. For example, assert that gasUsed is less than one hundred thousand units for a simple withdraw function, or check that a refactor doesn't increase gas beyond an acceptable delta. Log gasUsed during local runs to build a baseline before asserting. A common misconception is to use gas assertions as the only indicator of efficiency; gas checks complement profiling tools and should flag regressions but not replace in-depth performance analysis. Also remember that gas costs can depend on storage layout and prior state; ensure tests set up consistent conditions. The practical result: automated gas checks catch accidental expensive changes early and keep critical paths optimized.

keyIdea.title: Gas check pattern
keyIdea.text: Await the transaction receipt, read gasUsed, and assert it against a conservative threshold to detect regressions early.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.4 › Gas Cost Analysis
How to measure
Send tx, await receipt, read gasUsed, optionally multiply by effectiveGasPrice for cost.
const tx = await contract.doSomething();
const receipt = await tx.wait();
console.log("Gas used:", receipt.gasUsed.toString());
expect(receipt.gasUsed).to.be.lt(ethers.BigNumber.from("100000"));
Best practices
  • Establish a baseline by logging gas in local runs before setting thresholds.
  • Use conservative thresholds and avoid asserting exact numbers to account for minor variance.
  • Combine gas checks with profiling for deeper optimizations.
Watch out
Gas depends on prior state and storage layout. Ensure tests set consistent conditions to make comparisons meaningful.

screens.title: Mocking and stubbing external dependencies
screens.narratorSegment: Mocking replaces a full external dependency with a lightweight contract that implements only the functions you need for tests. Use mocking when deploying a full ERC20, oracle, or external protocol is unnecessary and slows tests. A simple mock provides predictable return values and can emit controlled events so you can test how your contract responds. For example, if your contract calls an oracle's latestAnswer function, deploy a mock that returns fixed values and allows you to simulate price changes by calling a setter. Another common case is token behavior: deploy a minimal ERC20 mock that supports transfer and balance inspection without full token economics. A misconception is that mocks remove the need to test integration against real implementations. They do not. Mocks are for focused unit tests; you should still run integration tests with real contracts when possible. Also avoid over-mocking: mocking too many interactions can give a false sense of correctness because the mock might not reflect real contract quirks. When designing a mock, only implement the functions your contract calls and include setter hooks to control outcomes in tests. This keeps tests fast, deterministic, and easy to reason about. The takeaway: mocks improve test focus and speed, but complement — not replace — integration verification.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.4 › Mocking & Stubbing
Why mock?
Control external behavior deterministically and avoid deploying heavy systems for unit tests.
Example: deploy a MockOracle with a setter to return a specific price, then test how your contract reacts to price changes without a full oracle deployment.
Guidelines
  • Implement only the interface your contract uses to keep the mock small.
  • Provide setter functions to simulate different external responses.
  • Complement mocks with at least some integration tests against real contracts.
Pro tip
Keep mocks minimal. When a mock grows large, consider if you should instead deploy a thin real implementation for integration tests.

screens.title: Testing complex interactions and state transitions
screens.narratorSegment: Complex contracts often act as state machines or orchestrate interactions across multiple contracts. Testing these flows requires building clear scenarios, controlling external actors, and asserting state transitions at each step. Start by mapping the states and transitions your contract supports — for an auction, states include accepting bids, ended, and settled. Create scenario cards for each major sequence: setup, participant actions, time manipulation, and final settlement. Use mocks for participants you don't want to fully emulate, snapshots to return to the configured scenario, and gas assertions to monitor expensive transitions. A practical approach is to write tests as short stories: arrange a scenario, act with specific accounts making calls that change state, capture receipts, and assert the expected state after each action. Include event assertions to ensure the contract not only changed storage but also emitted the right signals. A common misconception is to write a single long test that exercises every path; instead, split into focused tests for individual transitions to isolate regressions. Also be mindful of reentrancy and ordering: test malicious or unexpected sequences when relevant. For example, simulate addr1 placing a bid, then addr2 outbids and receives the refunded amount, then fast-forward time, end the auction, and verify the beneficiary receives funds and the AuctionEnded event fires. The core insight: test interactions by scripting realistic actor behavior, controlling the environment, and asserting state and events step by step.

Module 06 › Chapter 6.4 › Complex Interactions
State machine mapping
List states and transitions, then write focused tests for each transition with clear actor roles.
Scenario card: Auction cycle — bid, outbid with refund, fast-forward, endAuction, settle to beneficiary.
Scenario card: Vault lifecycle — deposit, attempt early withdraw, fast-forward, withdraw and emit event.
Testing tactics
  • Script realistic actor behavior in tests using multiple signers.
  • Use snapshots to return to configured states between scenarios.
  • Assert events, storage, and balances, accounting for gas where necessary.
Pro tip
Break long flows into smaller tests that validate a single transition; combine them in integration tests where appropriate.

screens.title: Auction: Full time-based test activity
screens.narratorSegment: The activity guides you through testing a simple Auction contract. Begin by deploying Auction with a bidding time and a beneficiary address. In the first test, fast-forward time past auctionEndTime and attempt to bid; expect the call to revert because the auction has ended. In the second test, attempt to call endAuction before auctionEndTime and expect a revert that enforces timing rules. For the full auction cycle test, use three signers: the beneficiary, addr1, and addr2. Have addr1 place an initial bid, then addr2 place a higher bid; the contract should return the previous highest bid to addr1. Capture balances and receipts as needed. Next call evm_increaseTime by bidding time plus one second and evm_mine to apply the timestamp. Then call endAuction, await the receipt, and assert that AuctionEnded emitted the correct winner and amount. Also assert that the beneficiary's balance increased by the highest bid, accounting for gas if the beneficiary is a signer in the test. A practical test practice is to use snapshots around the three-phase test so you can reuse the initial deployment. A common mistake in this exercise is forgetting to transfer or fund signers as needed before bidding; ensure signers have sufficient balance. Closing reflection: how would you structure tests if you needed to test dozens of bidding scenarios with different edge-case amounts? Consider snapshots and table-driven tests to scale coverage.

keyIdea.text: Simulate a real auction: test revert conditions, outbids and refunds, time fast-forward, and final settlement with event and balance assertions.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.4 › Auction Activity
Activity checklist
  1. Deploy Auction with 1-hour bidding time and beneficiary.
  2. Test revert when bidding after end by fast-forwarding time and mining.
  3. Test revert when ending auction too early.
  4. Simulate a full auction: addr1 bids, addr2 outbids, fast-forward, endAuction, assert event and balances.
Tip: Use ethers.getSigners() for multiple actors and ensure they have funds before bidding. Use snapshots to reuse a configured deployment for multiple scenario tests.
Starter test template
beforeEach(async function () {
  [owner, addr1, addr2] = await ethers.getSigners();
  Auction = await ethers.getContractFactory("Auction", owner);
  auction = await Auction.deploy(BIDDING_TIME, owner.address);
});

it("Should simulate a full auction cycle", async function () {
  await auction.connect(addr1).bid({ value: ethers.utils.parseEther("1") });
  await auction.connect(addr2).bid({ value: ethers.utils.parseEther("2") });
  await ethers.provider.send("evm_increaseTime", [BIDDING_TIME + 1]);
  await ethers.provider.send("evm_mine");
  const tx = await auction.connect(owner).endAuction();
  await expect(tx).to.emit(auction, "AuctionEnded");
});

screens.title: Common mistakes & test hygiene
screens.narratorSegment: Flaky tests are often caused by unaccounted gas costs, forgetting to mine after time changes, shared mutable state between tests, or mocks that do not reflect real behavior. Start by ensuring gas-aware assertions: when checking balances after a transaction, compute gasUsed times gasPrice and use a tolerant comparison such as closeTo. Next, always pair evm_increaseTime with evm_mine so the new timestamp is applied. For state isolation, use redeploys for small setups or snapshotting for large ones, and make sure to revert to the correct snapshot id in afterEach. When using mocks, keep them minimal and occasionally run integration tests with real dependencies to catch mismatches. Another source of flakiness is implicit dependencies on chain ordering or previous tests; write tests that fully arrange their needed preconditions or use snapshots to guarantee state. Use logging while developing tests to gather gas baselines and unexpected values, then remove or reduce logs in CI. Finally, write small focused tests for single behaviors and larger integration-style tests for orchestration paths; this division makes debugging easier. A short checklist helps: account for gas, mine after time changes, isolate state, validate mocks, and split long flows. Now ask: which flaky test in your suite matches one of these root causes, and which pattern will you apply to fix it?

keyIdea.text: Account for gas, mine after changing time, isolate state with redeploy or snapshots, and validate mocks with integration tests.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.4 › Common Mistakes
Top causes of flaky tests
  • Forgetting evm_mine after evm_increaseTime so timestamps don't apply.
  • Making exact balance assertions without accounting for gas.
  • Shared mutable state between tests due to missing snapshots or redeploys.
  • Mismatched behavior between mocks and real contracts.
Checklist to fix a flaky test
1) Re-check whether the test needs a mined block after time change. 2) Convert balance equality to a closeTo with gas accounted. 3) Isolate state by snapshotting or redeploying. 4) Replace or augment mocks with a thin real implementation if behavior differs.
Quick win
Switch a fragile exact balance assertion to a closeTo check that deducts gas. Many failing tests recover with this single change.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we build a practical toolkit for testing harder smart contract scenarios. You will learn how to manipulate blockchain time, take and restore EVM snapshots for fast isolated tests, measure gas in assertions, and mock external dependencies so tests stay focused and reliable. These techniques matter because real contracts often depend on time windows, on-chain state machines, or external services; naive tests miss subtle failures or become slow and flaky. For example, a time-locked vault must be tested both before and after an unlock timestamp; using the Hardhat RPC methods for advancing time and mining a block lets you simulate that passage reliably. Snapshotting saves a configured global state once and reverts to it between tests, making large setups fast to reuse. Gas checks in tests help you catch regressions in critical functions, and lightweight mocks let you control or simulate token transfers or oracle responses without deploying full systems. As you study the examples and activity, watch for common mistakes, like forgetting to mine after increasing time or neglecting to account for gas when checking balances. By the end you'll be able to pick the right pattern for time-based logic, costly setups, gas-sensitive functions, and external interactions. Consider where each technique could make your own test suite faster, less flaky, and more trustworthy.

Over the next screens we focus on four practical objectives. First, implement tests for time-dependent logic: you will learn how to change the EVM timestamp and mine a block so contracts that depend on block time behave predictably in tests. Second, apply EVM snapshotting to create fast, isolated test scenarios for expensive setups; you'll save state once and revert for each test to avoid redeploying complex systems. Third, write tests that simulate gas cost analysis: capture gas used in receipts and assert thresholds so critical functions don't regress. Fourth, explore strategies for testing interactions and when to use mocking or stubbing; mocks allow you to isolate your contract from full external dependencies. Each objective includes a short mnemonic to help embed the idea: think 'Time then Mine', 'Snapshot and Revert', 'Measure Gas', and 'Mock for Focus'. These skills reduce flakiness, speed up CI runs, and make test failures easier to diagnose. By the end you'll be able to plan a test strategy for common contract patterns like vaults, auctions, and factory systems.

This screen maps the objective skills to concrete test tasks you will perform. You will practice writing a test that attempts to withdraw from a time-locked vault before unlock and expects a revert, then fast-forward time and successfully withdraw while asserting balances and events. You will also build a test harness that uses EVM snapshotting: set up a costly factory once, snapshot the state, then revert between tests to reuse that configuration efficiently. For gas analysis, you will capture a transaction receipt and assert its gasUsed is below a chosen threshold to catch performance regressions. Finally, for mocking, you will deploy a minimal mock token or oracle implementing only the called functions so tests can deterministically control responses. Each objective includes a brief two-line mnemonic and a verified milestone, so you can check your progress. These capabilities help you write precise, fast, and maintainable tests that mirror real contract behavior without running long or producing flaky outcomes. Think about how each pattern reduces a different kind of test pain: time ambiguity, slow setup, unexpected gas spikes, and brittle external dependencies.

Temporal logic appears whenever a contract checks block timestamps or block numbers. A reliable test pattern has a few steps: detect the time-dependent requirement, arrange initial state, advance the EVM time, mine a block to apply the change, and then assert behavior and emitted events. Start by identifying the time boundary—unlockTime, auctionEndTime, or a vesting cliff. Arrange the contract in the desired pre-condition by calling deposit or placing bids so the state is meaningful. Then use the Hardhat RPC call to increase the EVM time by the required duration. Remember that increasing time alone does not change the chain until you mine a block; you must call the provider's mine method to create a block with the new timestamp. After mining, re-check the contract state and perform the action you want to test, such as withdraw or endAuction. Finally, assert on state changes, events, and balances. Include gas accounting if balance assertions are sensitive to gas costs. A common misconception is assuming that evm_increaseTime immediately changes block. timestamp without mining; tests that miss the mine step will silently fail to exercise the time condition. As a concrete example, take a vault with unlockTime set to now plus seven days: deposit funds, attempt withdrawal to confirm revert, evm_increaseTime by seven days plus one second, evm_mine, then withdraw and assert lockedAmount is zero, the recipient received funds, and a FundsUnlocked event fired. The key takeaway: always mine a block after changing time and include gas-aware assertions when verifying balances to avoid flaky tests.

Let's walk through a concrete test for the TimeLockVault contract. The test first deploys the contract with a seven-day lock and deposits funds so there is a meaningful lockedAmount. The first assertion attempts a withdrawal immediately and expects a revert with the message 'Funds are still locked'. This verifies the precondition. The second test simulates waiting by calling the provider's evm_increaseTime with the lock duration plus one second, then calls evm_mine to ensure the next block reflects the new timestamp. After mining, the test calls withdraw and awaits the transaction receipt. From the receipt it obtains gasUsed and multiplies by the effectiveGasPrice to measure the cost deducted from the owner's balance. The test then asserts that lockedAmount is zero, that the owner's balance increased by the withdrawn amount minus gas used using a closeTo assertion, and that the FundsUnlocked event was emitted with expected arguments. A key point is the gas-aware balance assertion: because the owner pays gas on withdraw, exact equality will fail; using closeTo with a small delta prevents flaky failures. A common misconception is to compare raw balances without subtracting gas or using a tolerant comparison. Another important detail is deploying contracts and calling deposit in beforeEach so each test starts with its own fresh contract state. Reflect: when would you prefer snapshotting over redeploying? That question guides the next pattern we explore.

EVM snapshotting saves the current state of the Hardhat Network so you can revert to it later. The typical pattern is to perform an expensive setup once in a global before hook — for example, deploy a factory and preload data — then call evm_snapshot just before a test, store the returned snapshot id, and after the test call evm_revert with that id. Reverting returns the chain to the exact saved state, making each test start from identical conditions without redeploying everything. This approach is much faster than running the full setup in beforeEach for heavy configurations. A concrete example: deploy a complex marketplace in before, then in beforeEach call snapshot and in afterEach revert. One misconception is to rely solely on before for setup and skip snapshotting; that causes tests to run against modified shared state and introduces interdependence and flakiness. Another mistake is using snapshots incorrectly by forgetting to reassign a new snapshot id for each test, which can lead to reverting to an older state inadvertently. Snapshotting is especially valuable when combined with other patterns: use snapshots after you arrange a preconfigured scenario, then within individual tests you can safely manipulate time, mock dependencies, or assert gas without worrying about cleanup. Remember that snapshots are a testing-only convenience provided by the Hardhat Network and are not available in production environments.

This lesson demonstrates a practical snapshot usage pattern inside a describe block. Run expensive setup once in a before hook: deploy a factory, configure roles, or mint many tokens. Then in beforeEach call the provider's evm_snapshot and store the returned id in a variable. This makes the following test start from the exact configured state. After each test, call evm_revert passing the snapshot id to return to the pre-test state. This pattern avoids redeploying heavy contracts repeatedly while still giving each test a clean slate. A concrete scenario: deploy a marketplace with multiple collections and liquidity in before, take a snapshot in beforeEach, then in tests modify balances, run auctions, or change approvals without affecting other tests because afterEach reverts the chain. One nuance: if a test itself calls evm_snapshot, track and revert that snapshot before returning to the suite-level snapshot. Another mistake is to reuse a single global snapshot id across multiple tests without reassigning it in beforeEach; this causes tests to rollback to an old state and can be confusing. Snapshotting pairs well with time manipulation and mocks: take the snapshot after mocking and configuring the scenario, then within the test you can fast-forward time or alter mocked return values and revert afterward. The closing question: which part of your current slow test setup could become a one-time before hook followed by snapshots?

Both snapshotting and redeploying beforeEach yield isolated tests, but they trade off speed and reproducibility differently. Redeploying in beforeEach gives each test a completely fresh set of contracts and is conceptually simple. It is ideal for small setups where deployment is cheap and you want maximum isolation. Snapshotting, by contrast, is a performance optimization: deploy or configure a large system once, take a snapshot, and revert to it between tests. This is much faster for complex environments but requires careful snapshot id management. A concrete example highlights the trade: a test suite that deploys a multi-contract factory and populates it with many tokens will grow slow if redeployed for every test. Using a before hook to build the system and snapshotting in beforeEach makes individual tests run quickly. A common misconception is that snapshotting reduces the need to design isolated tests; it does not. Snapshots restore state but do not replace good test boundaries. Another mistake is using snapshots when deployments are cheap; you risk adding complexity without a speed benefit. When deciding, ask: is the setup expensive and identical across tests? If yes, snapshot. If each test requires a different deployment configuration, redeploying in beforeEach is clearer and safer. The final takeaway: choose the simpler approach unless performance demands the optimization.

Gas analysis in tests helps you prevent regressions in critical contract functions. The common pattern is to send a transaction, wait for its receipt, read receipt. gasUsed, and compare that value against a chosen threshold. Start by identifying functions where gas matters — loops, token transfers in batches, or frequently called public functions. In your test, call the function, await tx. wait(), and then read receipt. gasUsed. If you want to analyze cost in currency terms, multiply gasUsed by receipt. effectiveGasPrice to compute the native token cost. Be cautious: gas numbers can vary slightly across environments, so assert conservative thresholds rather than exact numbers. For example, assert that gasUsed is less than one hundred thousand units for a simple withdraw function, or check that a refactor doesn't increase gas beyond an acceptable delta. Log gasUsed during local runs to build a baseline before asserting. A common misconception is to use gas assertions as the only indicator of efficiency; gas checks complement profiling tools and should flag regressions but not replace in-depth performance analysis. Also remember that gas costs can depend on storage layout and prior state; ensure tests set up consistent conditions. The practical result: automated gas checks catch accidental expensive changes early and keep critical paths optimized.

Mocking replaces a full external dependency with a lightweight contract that implements only the functions you need for tests. Use mocking when deploying a full ERC20, oracle, or external protocol is unnecessary and slows tests. A simple mock provides predictable return values and can emit controlled events so you can test how your contract responds. For example, if your contract calls an oracle's latestAnswer function, deploy a mock that returns fixed values and allows you to simulate price changes by calling a setter. Another common case is token behavior: deploy a minimal ERC20 mock that supports transfer and balance inspection without full token economics. A misconception is that mocks remove the need to test integration against real implementations. They do not. Mocks are for focused unit tests; you should still run integration tests with real contracts when possible. Also avoid over-mocking: mocking too many interactions can give a false sense of correctness because the mock might not reflect real contract quirks. When designing a mock, only implement the functions your contract calls and include setter hooks to control outcomes in tests. This keeps tests fast, deterministic, and easy to reason about. The takeaway: mocks improve test focus and speed, but complement — not replace — integration verification.

Complex contracts often act as state machines or orchestrate interactions across multiple contracts. Testing these flows requires building clear scenarios, controlling external actors, and asserting state transitions at each step. Start by mapping the states and transitions your contract supports — for an auction, states include accepting bids, ended, and settled. Create scenario cards for each major sequence: setup, participant actions, time manipulation, and final settlement. Use mocks for participants you don't want to fully emulate, snapshots to return to the configured scenario, and gas assertions to monitor expensive transitions. A practical approach is to write tests as short stories: arrange a scenario, act with specific accounts making calls that change state, capture receipts, and assert the expected state after each action. Include event assertions to ensure the contract not only changed storage but also emitted the right signals. A common misconception is to write a single long test that exercises every path; instead, split into focused tests for individual transitions to isolate regressions. Also be mindful of reentrancy and ordering: test malicious or unexpected sequences when relevant. For example, simulate addr1 placing a bid, then addr2 outbids and receives the refunded amount, then fast-forward time, end the auction, and verify the beneficiary receives funds and the AuctionEnded event fires. The core insight: test interactions by scripting realistic actor behavior, controlling the environment, and asserting state and events step by step.

The activity guides you through testing a simple Auction contract. Begin by deploying Auction with a bidding time and a beneficiary address. In the first test, fast-forward time past auctionEndTime and attempt to bid; expect the call to revert because the auction has ended. In the second test, attempt to call endAuction before auctionEndTime and expect a revert that enforces timing rules. For the full auction cycle test, use three signers: the beneficiary, addr1, and addr2. Have addr1 place an initial bid, then addr2 place a higher bid; the contract should return the previous highest bid to addr1. Capture balances and receipts as needed. Next call evm_increaseTime by bidding time plus one second and evm_mine to apply the timestamp. Then call endAuction, await the receipt, and assert that AuctionEnded emitted the correct winner and amount. Also assert that the beneficiary's balance increased by the highest bid, accounting for gas if the beneficiary is a signer in the test. A practical test practice is to use snapshots around the three-phase test so you can reuse the initial deployment. A common mistake in this exercise is forgetting to transfer or fund signers as needed before bidding; ensure signers have sufficient balance. Closing reflection: how would you structure tests if you needed to test dozens of bidding scenarios with different edge-case amounts? Consider snapshots and table-driven tests to scale coverage.

Flaky tests are often caused by unaccounted gas costs, forgetting to mine after time changes, shared mutable state between tests, or mocks that do not reflect real behavior. Start by ensuring gas-aware assertions: when checking balances after a transaction, compute gasUsed times gasPrice and use a tolerant comparison such as closeTo. Next, always pair evm_increaseTime with evm_mine so the new timestamp is applied. For state isolation, use redeploys for small setups or snapshotting for large ones, and make sure to revert to the correct snapshot id in afterEach. When using mocks, keep them minimal and occasionally run integration tests with real dependencies to catch mismatches. Another source of flakiness is implicit dependencies on chain ordering or previous tests; write tests that fully arrange their needed preconditions or use snapshots to guarantee state. Use logging while developing tests to gather gas baselines and unexpected values, then remove or reduce logs in CI. Finally, write small focused tests for single behaviors and larger integration-style tests for orchestration paths; this division makes debugging easier. A short checklist helps: account for gas, mine after time changes, isolate state, validate mocks, and split long flows. Now ask: which flaky test in your suite matches one of these root causes, and which pattern will you apply to fix it?

Let's summarize the essential concepts. Time-dependent logic relies on block timestamps or numbers; always use evm_increaseTime followed by evm_mine to simulate time reliably. EVM snapshotting, using evm_snapshot and evm_revert, saves and restores the chain state to speed up tests around a heavy setup. Gas cost analysis uses transaction receipts and receipt. gasUsed to assert gas thresholds and catch regressions early. Mocking creates small controlled contract stand-ins for external dependencies, improving speed and determinism in unit tests, but should be complemented with integration tests. Keep these techniques in mind and combine them: snapshot after configuring mocks, then fast-forward time and run gas checks within isolated tests. Each technique addresses a specific testing pain point and together they form a practical toolkit for robust smart contract testing. Which pattern will you add to your toolkit first?

To close, remember these operational rules. Always mine a block after advancing time. When checking balances after transactions, subtract or account for gas and prefer tolerant comparisons. Use evm_snapshot and evm_revert to speed up tests with heavy setups, but don't let snapshot complexity hide poor test design. Mock external systems to control behavior in unit tests, and complement mocks with integration tests using real implementations where practical. Finally, log gas usage locally to build baselines before asserting thresholds in CI. These practices together will make your test suite faster, less flaky, and better at catching real regressions. As you integrate these patterns into your workflow, pick one to adopt first and measure the improvement in test time and reliability. What to Remember means mine after increasing time, account for gas in assertions, snapshot heavy setups, mock when appropriate, and verify with integration tests..
